title: Classes and Objects
summary: Data, sealed, enum, object and companion, inheritance, interfaces, and value classes.

lesson.heading: Inheritance: final by default
lesson.body:
In Kotlin, classes and methods are **final by default**: to extend them you need `open` on the class and on the member, and `override` in the subclass. An `override` is itself open, unless you mark it `final override`.

The default visibility is `public`; there are also `internal` (same module), `protected`, and `private`. `abstract` classes are implicitly open.

lesson.heading: Data classes
lesson.body:
A `data class` generates `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy`, and the `componentN` functions for destructuring, but **only for the properties in the primary constructor**. Properties declared in the body are ignored by `equals`.

`copy()` is a **shallow** copy: referenced objects (a `MutableList`, for example) are shared. A data class can't be `open`, `abstract`, `sealed`, or `inner`, but it can extend classes and implement interfaces.
lesson.code:
data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)

val u = User(1, "Ann")
val v = u.copy(name = "Bea")
val (id, name) = v
println(v) // User(id=1, name=Bea)

lesson.heading: Sealed vs enum
lesson.body:
An `enum` has a fixed set of **instances**, all with the same structure. A `sealed class` or `sealed interface` has a fixed set of **subtypes**, each with its own data and potentially many instances.

Both allow an exhaustive `when` without `else`: adding a case breaks compilation wherever it needs handling. The subtypes of a sealed type must live in the same module and package. They're ideal for UI states and results (`Loading`, `Success(data)`, `Error(msg)`).

lesson.heading: object and companion object
lesson.body:
`object` declares a **singleton**, initialized lazily and thread-safely on first access. `data object` adds a readable `toString` and is handy in sealed hierarchies.

A `companion object` holds members accessed through the class name, replacing Java statics, and is often used for factories and constants. To expose them to Java as true statics, use `@JvmStatic` or `const val`.

lesson.heading: Interfaces and value classes
lesson.body:
Interfaces can have methods with default implementations and properties that are abstract or have getters, but **no state** (no backing fields). A class can implement many of them while extending only one class.

A `@JvmInline value class` wraps a single value, giving you type safety (e.g. `UserId` vs `String`) with no runtime allocation in most cases. It does get **boxed**, though, when used as a generic type, as an interface, or, if the underlying type is primitive, as a nullable.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Classic question: **"What's the difference between a data class, a sealed class, and an enum?"** Short answer: a data class is a data holder with equals/hashCode/copy generated from the primary constructor; an enum is a closed set of instances; a sealed class is a closed set of types, each with its own data.

Mention the exhaustive `when`, that `object` is a thread-safe singleton, and that classes are final by default, a choice that favors composition over inheritance.

questions.prompt: By default, a Kotlin class is:
questions.explanation: Classes are final (you need `open` to extend them) and the default visibility is public.
whyWrong: Public, yes, but not open: Kotlin classes are final by default, and you have to explicitly mark them `open` to extend them.
Final is right, but the default visibility is public; `internal` (visible only within the module) has to be declared explicitly.
Both halves are flipped: by default a class is final (not open) and public (not internal).

questions.explanation: The generated `equals` only considers primary constructor properties: `age` is in the body and gets ignored.
whyWrong: Different ages suggest different objects, but `age` is declared in the body, and the generated `equals` only compares `name`, which is the same in both.
A data class can have properties in its body, and `apply` works on any object: the code compiles just fine.
`==` calls `equals`, not `hashCode`; and in any case both generated methods only consider `name`, so the result is deterministic: true.

questions.code:
data class Team(val members: MutableList<String>)

val t1 = Team(mutableListOf("A"))
val t2 = t1.copy()
t2.members.add("B")
println(t1.members.size)
questions.explanation: `copy()` is shallow: t1 and t2 share the same MutableList, so the addition is visible from t1 too.
whyWrong: It looks like `copy()` creates a new list, but it only copies the reference: t1 and t2 point to the same `MutableList`, which now has 2 elements.
Nothing gets removed: t1 starts with "A" and also sees "B" through the shared list, so the size is 2.
`copy()` doesn't throw, and `add` on a `MutableList` is perfectly legal: the code runs and prints 2.

questions.prompt: How do you declare a singleton in Kotlin?
questions.explanation: An `object` declaration creates a singleton that's initialized lazily and thread-safely.
whyWrong: Kotlin has no `static` keyword: you use `object` and `companion object` instead.
`singleton` isn't a Kotlin keyword: you declare a singleton with `object Foo`.
There's `companion object` inside a class, not `companion class`: for a top-level singleton, `object Foo` is all you need.

questions.prompt: What's the main advantage of a sealed hierarchy in a `when`?
options: A when expression is exhaustive without else
It can be extended from any module
questions.explanation: The compiler knows every subtype, so the `when` is exhaustive and a new case produces errors wherever it needs handling.
whyWrong: Subclasses of a sealed type can be `object`s, but also classes or data classes with many instances: they aren't required to be singletons.
It's the opposite: the direct subclasses of a sealed type must live in the same module and package, precisely because the compiler has to know all of them.
It's not about performance: the benefit is compiler-checked exhaustiveness in `when`, which enums get too, for that matter.

questions.prompt: Given `@JvmInline value class Meters(val v: Int)`, in which case does Meters get boxed?
questions.explanation: When used as a generic argument, the value class has to be boxed; as a direct parameter or return type it's represented as an Int.
whyWrong: As a direct parameter, `Meters` is represented as an `Int` (with the function name mangled): no boxing.
A variable of the exact type `Meters` stays a plain `Int` in the bytecode: boxing kicks in with generics, nullable types, or supertypes.
Even as a direct return type, the value class is "unwrapped" into an `Int`; boxing is needed when it's used as a generic argument, a nullable, or a supertype.

options: It creates a second instance of the class
It defines an extension of the class
It holds members accessed through the class name
questions.explanation: It's the idiomatic equivalent of static members: factories, constants, and helpers accessed as `ClassName.member`.
whyWrong: There's only one companion object per class, and it's an object in its own right: it isn't a second instance of the enclosing class.
It has no effect on abstractness: a class only becomes abstract with `abstract`, and it can have a companion object either way.
Extensions are declared with `fun ClassName.name()`; the companion is a nested object (if anything, you can define extensions on the companion itself).

questions.prompt: Which statement about data classes is true?
options: It must have at least two properties
It can extend an open class and implement interfaces
questions.explanation: A data class can't be open/abstract/sealed/inner, but it can extend classes and implement interfaces. One constructor property is enough.
whyWrong: A data class can't be `open`, `abstract`, `sealed`, or `inner`: the generated `equals` wouldn't hold up with subclasses.
A single property in the primary constructor is enough: the requirement is at least one, not two.
The generated `equals` only uses primary constructor properties; the ones declared in the body are ignored.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a sealed class over an enum?
options: When the cases carry different data or have multiple instances
questions.explanation: An enum has fixed instances with the same structure; a sealed type allows subtypes with their own data, like Success(data) and Error(msg).
whyWrong: For a fixed set of constants, an enum is the natural choice: a sealed type becomes useful when the cases carry different data.
`ordinal` is an enum feature, not a sealed class one: if you need it, an enum is the right choice.
`entries` is generated for enums, and sealed classes don't offer it: if anything, that's a reason to prefer the enum.

options: Doesn't compile: no properties in interfaces
questions.explanation: Interfaces can have properties with default getters (no backing field). `greeting` uses P's `name`.
whyWrong: `name` isn't null: it's an abstract property that P implements with "Bo", and the default getter reads it at call time.
Kotlin interfaces can declare properties, either abstract or with default getters; what they can't have is a backing field.
The `greeting` getter is evaluated on every access, when `name` is already "Bo": there's no initialization-order issue at all.
